source_text: Μιᾶς τοίνυν οὔσης τῆς ἀληθείας (τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος μυρίας ἐκτροπὰς ἔχει), καθάπερ αἱ βάκχαι τὰ τοῦ Πενθέως διαφορήσασαι μέλη αἱ τῆς φιλοσοφίας τῆς τε βαρβάρου τῆς τε Ἑλληνικῆς αἱρέσεις, ἑκάστη ὅπερ ἔλαχεν ὡς πᾶσαν αὐχεῖ τὴν ἀλήθειαν· φωτὸς δ’, οἶμαι, ἀνατολῇ πάντα φωτίζεται. ξύμπαντες οὖν Ἕλληνές τε καὶ βάρβαροι, ὅσοι τἀληθοῦς ὠρέχθησαν, οἳ μὲν οὐκ ὀλίγα, οἳ δὲ μέρος τι, εἴπερ ἄρα, τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγου ἔχοντες ἂν δειχθεῖεν. ὁ γοῦν αἰὼν τοῦ χρόνου τὸ μέλλον καὶ τὸ ἐνεστός, ἀτὰρ δὴ καὶ τὸ παρῳχηκὸς ἀκαριαίως συνίστησι, πολὺ δὲ πλέον δυνατωτέρα τοῦ αἰῶνος ἡ ἀλήθεια συναγαγεῖν τὰ οἰκεῖα σπέρματα, κἂν εῖς τὴν ἀλλοδαπὴν ἐκπέσῃ γῆν. πάμπολλα γὰρ τῶν παρὰ ταῖς αἱρέσεσι δοξαζομένων εὕροιμεν ἄν (ὅσαι μὴ τέλεον ἐκκεκώφηνται μηδὲ ἐξετμήθησαν τὴν φυσικὴν ἀκολουθίαν, καθάπερ τὸν ἄνδρα αἱ γυναικωνίτιδες ἀποκοψάμεναι τὸν λόγον), εἰ καὶ ἀλλήλοις ἀνόμοια εἶναι δοκεῖ, τῷ γένει γε καὶ ὅλῃ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ὁμολογοῦντα· ἢ γὰρ ὡς μέλος ἢ ὡς μέρος ἢ ὡς εἶδος ἢ ὡς γένος εἰς ἕν συνάπτεται. ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἡ ὑπάτη ἐναντία τῇ νεάτῃ οὖσα. ἀλλ’ ἄμφω γε ἁρμονία μία, ἔν τε ἀριθμοῖς ὁ ἄρτιος τῷ περιττῷ διαφέρεται, ὁμολογοῦσι δὲ ἄμφω τῇ ἀριθμητικῇ, ὡς τῷ σχήματι ὁ κύκλος καὶ τὸ τρίγωνον καὶ τὸ τετράγωνον καὶ ὅσα τῶν σχημάτων ἀλλήλων διενήνοχεν. ἀτὰρ καὶ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ παντὶ τά μέρη σύμπαντα, κἂν διαφέρηται πρὸς ἄλληλα, τὴν πρὸς τὸ ὅλον οἰκειότητα διαφυλάττει. οὕτως οὖν ἥ τε βάρβαρος ἥ τε Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία τὴν ἀίδιον ἀλήθειαν σπαραγμόν τινα, οὐ τῆς Διονύσου μυθολογίας, τῆς δὲ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ ὄντος ἀεὶ θεολογίας πεποίηται. ὁ δὲ τὰ διῃρημένα συνθεὶς αὖθις καὶ ἑνοποιήσας τέλειον τὸν λόγον ἀκινδύνως εὖ ἴσθ’ ὅτι κατόψεται τὴν ἀλήθειαν. γέγραπται γοῦν ἐν τῷ Ἐκκλησιαστῇ· καὶ προσέθηκα σοφίαν ἐπὶ πᾶσιν, οἳ δὴ ἐγένοντο ἔμπροσθέν μου ἐν Ἱερουσαλήμ· καὶ ἡ καρδία μου εἶδεν πολλά, σοφίαν καὶ γνῶσιν, παραβολὰς καὶ ἐπιστήμην ἔγνων. ὅτι καί γε τοῦτό ἐστι προαίρεσις πνεύματος, ὅτι ἐν πλήθει σοφίας πλῆθος γνώσεως. ὁ δὲ τῆς παντοδαπῆς σοφίας ἔμπειρος, οὗτος κυρίως ἂν εἴη γνωστικός. αὐτίκα γέγραπται· περισσεία γνώσεως τῆς σοφίας ζωοποιήσει τὸν παρ’ αὐτῆς. πάλιν τε αὖ βεβαιοῖ σαφέστερον τὰ εἰρημένα ἥδε ἡ ῥῆσις· πάντα ἐνώπια τοῖς νοοῦσι (τὰ δὲ πάντα Ἑλληνικά ἐστι καὶ βαρβαρικά, θάτερα δὲ οὐκέτι πάντα), ὀρθὰ δὲ τοῖς βουλομένοις ἀπενέγκασθαι αἴσθησιν. ἀνθαιρεῖσθε παιδείαν καὶ μὴ ἀργύριον καὶ μὴ ἀργύριον, καὶ γνῶσιν ὑπὲρ χρυσίον δεδοκιμασμένον, ἀνθαιρεῖσθε δὲ καὶ αἴσθησιν χρυσίου καθαροῦ· κρείσσων γὰρ σοφία λίθων πολυτελῶν, πᾶν δὲ τίμιον οὐκ ἄξιον αὐτῆς.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, since there is one truth (for falsehood has many deviations), just as the Bacchae tore apart the limbs of Pentheus, the sects of philosophy, both barbarian and Greek, each boast that they have the whole truth; but, I think, with the rising of light, everything is illuminated. So, all Greeks and barbarians who have desired the truth, some having much, some having a part, if indeed they have any of the word of truth, would be shown. For time brings together the future and the present, and also the past, without trouble, but truth is much more powerful than time to gather its own seeds, even if they fall into foreign soil. For we would find many things that are glorified by the sects (as long as they have not been completely mutilated or cut off from the natural sequence, just like the man whose reason has been cut off by women's chatter), even if they seem to be unlike each other, yet they agree with the whole truth in genus and in entirety; either as a part or as a whole or as a species or as a genus, they are connected to one. And already the highest and the lowest are opposites. But both are in harmony, just as in numbers the even and the odd differ, yet both agree with arithmetic, just as the circle and the triangle and the square and all the shapes that are connected to each other. And in the whole world, all the parts, even if they differ from each other, preserve their relationship to the whole. So, both barbarian and Greek philosophy have made a kind of tearing apart, not of the mythology of Dionysus, but of the theology of the eternal word. And the one who gathers the divided things and unites them again will, without danger, know the truth well. For it is written in Ecclesiastes: I added wisdom to all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my heart saw many things, wisdom and knowledge, parables and science, I knew. For this is also a choice of spirit, that in a multitude of wisdom there is a multitude of knowledge. And the one who is experienced in all kinds of wisdom would be a gnostic in the true sense. Immediately it is written: the abundance of knowledge of wisdom will give life to the one who is near it. And again, this statement confirms more clearly what was said: all things are manifest to those who understand (and all things are Greek and barbarian, but not all things are other), and it is right to bring perception to those who wish. You are buying education, not silver, and knowledge that has been tested more than gold, and you are buying perception of pure gold; for wisdom is better than precious stones, and everything valuable is not worthy of it.
pass_b_english: Since there is only one truth—for falsehood has countless deviations—the sects of philosophy, both barbarian and Greek, tear truth apart like the Bacchae tearing the limbs of Pentheus, each boasting that it possesses the whole truth. Yet I think that when light rises, everything is illuminated. So all Greeks and barbarians who have longed for the truth, some holding much of it, some a portion—if indeed they hold any of the word of truth—would be shown to have it. For time gathers the future and the present, and also the past, without trouble; but truth is far more powerful than time to gather its own seeds, even if they fall into foreign soil. Indeed, we would find many things celebrated among the sects—provided they have not been completely mutilated or severed from their natural sequence, like a man whose reason is cut off by women's chatter—that, even though they seem unlike one another, nonetheless agree with the whole truth in genus and in entirety. Whether as a limb, a part, a species, or a genus, each is joined to the one. Even the highest and lowest notes are opposites, yet both belong to a single harmony. Just as in numbers the even and the odd differ, yet both submit to arithmetic; and just as the circle, triangle, square, and every other figure, though distinct, share in geometry. And in the whole world, all the parts, even when they differ from one another, preserve their relationship to the whole. Thus both barbarian and Greek philosophy have made a kind of dismemberment—not of the mythology of Dionysus, but of the theology of the eternal Word. But the one who gathers the divided things and unites them again will, without danger, see the truth clearly. For it is written in Ecclesiastes: 'I added wisdom to all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my heart saw many things—wisdom and knowledge, parables and science—I knew them' (Eccl 1:16–17 LXX). For this too is a choice of the Spirit: that in a multitude of wisdom there is a multitude of knowledge. And the one who is experienced in every kind of wisdom would be a gnostic in the true sense. Immediately it is written: 'The abundance of the knowledge of wisdom will give life to the one who is near it' (Eccl 1:18 LXX). And again this saying confirms what was said more clearly: 'All things are manifest to those who understand'—and all things are Greek and barbarian, but the rest are no longer all things—and 'it is right to bring perception to those who wish' (Prov 8:9 LXX). Buy education, not silver; buy knowledge tested more than gold; buy perception of pure gold. For wisdom is better than precious stones, and nothing valuable is worthy of it (Prov 8:10–11 LXX).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished, readable version that correctly identifies and expands the scripture citations (Ecclesiastes and Proverbs) which were alluded to in the Greek. All clauses, including the parenthetical remarks and the mathematical analogies, are preserved.
